content: Treatment services are a critical aspect of healthcare delivery. Simplifying methods to assess hepatitis C virus (HCV) viral load and genotype, as well as tests to monitor drug toxicity, is essential to improve treatment accessibility in resource-limited settings. Planning for new treatment centers should include pharmacy facilities and adequate drug storage, including refrigeration for interferon (IFN). Additionally, sourcing and distribution logistics must be carefully planned. The registration of new drugs in individual countries can be time-consuming and requires thorough preparation. Key components of service delivery include sufficient clinic infrastructure, laboratory and diagnostic services, a reliable drug supply, trained healthcare professionals (including doctors, nurses, and psychological support providers), referral systems, monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, and the involvement of civil society. Expanding access to treatment necessitates identifying infected individuals, prioritizing HCV screening, and targeting high-risk populations. Once diagnosed, patients with HCV require access to medical facilities for treatment, ongoing follow-up, and monitoring for drug toxicity and efficacy. Integrating HCV services with existing programs, such as those for HIV, can provide additional benefits. Standardized and simplified treatment regimens at the population level can facilitate service delivery. Decentralized service models, which have proven effective in treating large numbers of HIV-infected individuals, should be adopted for HCV. These models should utilize simplified operational guidelines, training materials, clinical decision-making tools, and limited formularies. Before initiating therapy, a comprehensive clinical assessment is necessary to identify pre-existing conditions that may delay or contraindicate treatment, such as severe intercurrent illnesses, decompensated cirrhosis, tuberculosis (TB), or pregnancy. Psychological evaluations and assessments of potential drug-drug interactions are also critical. Patient education, preparation for treatment side effects, and informed preand post-test counseling are essential components of care. Treatment should employ standardized regimens alongside simplified clinical decision-making tools and monitoring protocols. Locally tailored care packages and treatment algorithms, including those for firstand second-generation direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), should be developed. These algorithms must address when to start and stop therapy, follow-up schedules, side effect management, and drug-drug interaction considerations, particularly in HIV co-infected individuals. For example, drugs like zidovudine (AZT), didanosine (ddI), and stavudine (d4T), commonly used in low-income settings, are not recommended for patients treated with IFN and ribavirin (RBV). Monitoring and evaluating treatment centers is vital for effective management. Standardized registers, similar to those used in TB treatment programs, can track progress and outcomes following the rollout of HCV treatment. Increased supervision of treatment sites is particularly important during the early stages of implementation. The landscape of HCV treatment is rapidly evolving, and adaptations will be necessary as new drugs are approved. Curative treatments with higher efficacy and lower toxicity have the potential to significantly reduce the global health and economic burdens of HCV infection. Achieving this goal will demand political commitment, financial investment, and collaboration among pharmaceutical companies, medical organizations, and civil society. The dissemination, monitoring, and implementation of guidelines for HCV screening, care, and treatment are crucial. These guidelines will be launched at international conferences and made accessible on the World Health Organization (WHO) website. Successful implementation will depend on careful adaptation and integration into regional and national strategies, supported by available resources, enabling policies, and partnerships. Ideally, the impact of these guidelines would be assessed by tracking the number of individuals treated and cured of HCV, although no national-level monitoring system currently exists to collect this data.
